## TL;DR

Close-out now uses the shared core default-branch resolver instead of a private resolver in the integration orchestrator. The shared resolver checks candidates in the intended order and returns a candidate only when its local `refs/heads/<name>` ref exists. If the remote default or configured init branch is stale, it continues through the checked-out branch and the conventional `main` and `master` fallbacks. If close-out still cannot resolve the branch to a commit, its failure reason now includes the selected branch, repository root, exit status, timeout state, and stderr. The close-out runbook and regression tests cover these behaviors.

## Work and rationale

The failure described for the tiao project came from treating `init.defaultBranch` as proof of a branch's existence. Git configuration can outlive the branch naming convention of an existing repository. In the reported case, `master` was configured as the default for newly initialized repositories, while the existing repository had `main` and no remote metadata. Returning `master` caused the subsequent commit lookup to fail.

The repository already had a shared resolver in `src/core/repo-log.ts`, so I extended that instead of adding another helper. The resolver now gathers the symbolic target of `refs/remotes/origin/HEAD`, the `init.defaultBranch` setting, and the checked-out branch, then checks each candidate using `git show-ref --verify --quiet refs/heads/<candidate>`. Invalid branch names and non-local refs are not accepted. The resolver next checks `main` and `master`. If neither conventional name exists, it uses the checked-out branch as the final fallback; an unborn repository remains represented by `HEAD`.

`src/server/integration-orchestrator.ts` imports the shared resolver and no longer contains its own implementation. This ensures all close-out phases use the same selection behavior and prevents another call site from silently retaining the unsafe configuration shortcut. In the synchronization phase, a failed `rev-parse <branch>^{commit}` now reports the attempted branch and root along with git's status, timeout flag, and stderr. I factored the diagnostic formatting into a small function so the exact failure information can be tested without manufacturing a timing-sensitive disappearing-ref race.

The regression tests exercise the originally reported configuration (a `main` branch with `init.defaultBranch=master` and no remote), a remote-less `trunk` repository, and an `origin/HEAD` target that has no corresponding local branch. A diagnostic test checks that the failure string carries all requested fields, including git stderr and exit status. The quick-reference row in `docs/close-out-pipeline.md` now directs operators to the specific branch and stderr details rather than recommending an uninformative retry.

## Approaches tried

I first inspected the existing shared implementation and the private close-out copy. The shared version only checked `main`, `master`, and then HEAD, while the private version trusted remote HEAD and `init.defaultBranch` without checking local refs. The chosen approach was to move the complete priority policy into the existing shared resolver, retaining the shared API used by repository history and branch listings, and delete the private copy.

I considered validating only the configured branch because that would fix the reported machine, but that would leave `origin/HEAD` capable of selecting a remote-only branch name. Instead, every discovered name passes through the same local-ref check. I also avoided making the failure diagnostic depend on a large mocked orchestration setup; the formatted reason is a focused pure helper, while real repository fixtures cover branch resolution.

## Challenges and blockers

The first local scoped check found a formatter issue in the resolver. I ran the repository formatter, then restarted the full requested check. That attempt completed the build, UI smoke, and other local steps, but its test suite hit a timeout in `agent-start-host-pressure.test.ts`; the code changes do not touch the pressure guard or engineer-start logic. Following `docs/debugging-check-failures.md`, I ran that test file alone. It passed all three tests, consistent with the repository's documented host-pressure timing failure mode.

I retried the scoped check. The remote validation initially spent an extended period uploading the incremental bundle, then completed on the `bee` runner. It passed the full scoped suite and the remote build and rendered checks. RepoOS then ran local-only guards and UI smoke, which also passed. No product or implementation blocker remained.

## Key learnings

Repository defaults have different meanings at different layers: `init.defaultBranch` is an initialization preference, and `origin/HEAD` is remote symbolic metadata. Neither guarantees that a local branch ref with that name exists now. A resolver should treat both as candidate hints and validate them against repository state before using them for commit operations.

Failure diagnostics at the point of the failed git command are more useful than a generic error or an automatic retry when the root cause is repository state. Naming the branch, root, status, timeout, and stderr gives an operator enough information to distinguish a missing ref from a timeout or another git failure.

Finally, the pressure test timeout demonstrated the value of this repository's triage rule: isolate the failing test and compare against its documented environmental failure class before changing unrelated code. The focused rerun and subsequent remote suite both passed, so no pressure-guard change was warranted.
